transcript.text: My Hotpoint washer dryer isn't drying properly any more and there's a funny smell when it's on the dry bit. Is there something I should clean?

Yes — cleaning is the right first step. Poor drying with a hot or odd smell is most often fluff/debris restricting the drying airflow or the route the condensed water drains through. A full wash load put straight onto dry can also leave clothes damp, even with no fault. If the smell is strongly burning, acrid, or you see any smoke, stop using it, switch it off and unplug it until it is fully cool. 1. With it switched off and unplugged, clean the pump filter at the lower front, if fitted. Put towels and a shallow tray down first, then open it slowly as water may come out. Remove fluff, hair, coins and debris. This helps the condensed water escape during drying. 2. Clean any user-accessible fluff filter, condenser/filter flap, and the door seal area. Remove fluff by hand or with a soft brush; do not force anything into ducts. Restricted airflow can make the heater run too hot and smell. 3. Check the cold-water tap is fully on and the inlet and drain hoses behind the machine are not kinked or crushed. Many washer-dryers use cold water during drying to condense moisture, then pump it away. 4. Try drying only a small load that has already been properly spun — roughly no more than the stated dry capacity, which is usually lower than the wash capacity. Use a normal full drying setting rather than a short timed option. If it gets hot but remains damp after those checks, a remaining restriction in the condensing/air path is more likely than the heater. If it stays cold, the drying heater, thermostat or thermal cut-out needs diagnosing by an engineer rather than replacing parts speculatively.

Hmm, it does smell like burning dust or scorched fabric, and the top of the machine gets very hot to touch. I think I saw a faint haze near the door seal once too. I've still been using it though. Should I carry on with those cleaning steps?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. A burning/scorched smell together with haze near the door seal is not normal, even though the top can become warm during drying. It needs a qualified appliance engineer to inspect it before it is used again. The most likely cause is fluff or a restriction in the drying/condensing route causing overheating, but a faulty drying heater control, fan, thermal protection or wiring also has to be ruled out. Cleaning accessible areas can still be worthwhile with the machine unplugged and fully cool, but it must not be treated as a repair or proof that it is safe to restart. Leave it unplugged. Do not remove panels or try to inspect internal heaters, wiring or ducts. When booking, report: poor drying, burning-dust/scorched-fabric smell, very hot cabinet top, and a faint haze seen by the door seal. The engineer should check the complete drying air/condensing path as well as the heater and overheat controls.

candidates: Fluff/debris restricting the drying airflow or water-condensing path (high)
Drying load too large or laundry insufficiently spun first (medium)
Drying heater thermostat or thermal cut-out fault (low)

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit.
